concept: Playing-card deck cutting collation and packaging automation
summary: Source-anchored research for Playing-card deck cutting collation and packaging automation. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Duplo lists an external waste bin for the DC-746; this is a manufacturer feature claim. (low confidence)
Lassco states that the CR-50 accepts Standard, Special and Large cutting units and includes one Standard unit. Tool selection is part of configuring the corner-rounding operation. (low confidence)

The Morgana Countron AT Touch page uses different mechanism labels: its descriptive paragraph says twin-blade counting, while its specification field says Pin & blade. Preserve both descriptions pending model-specific clarification. (low confidence)

Uchida describes EZC-250 batch counting and interval timing as helping an operator collect a designated number of items; it also describes automatic retry after a slipped feed. Treat operator collection as a labor step when evaluating this counter. (low confidence)
The AeroCut X manual warns that overfilled waste can cause errors or breakdown. Waste removal therefore belongs in the cutting workflow. (low confidence)
Duplo describes the DC-746 cutting mechanism as rotary slitters plus a guillotine cutter. (low confidence)
Horizon identifies the SmartSlitter registration camera as optional. Specify that option when evaluating an equipped system. (low confidence)

Duplo lists a DSC-10/60i input minimum of 4.1 x 5.8 inches and a maximum rated speed of 10,000 sets per hour. These are document-collator specifications, not demonstrated finished-card deck throughput; smaller finished cards require a different documented feeding solution. (low confidence)

Madison advertises card-line counting, stacking and banding for cards starting at 3 x 3 inches. Its SB-25 waits for a predetermined count or an upstream sort signal before banding; the advertised minimum size needs checking against the actual cards. (low confidence)
MBM’s AeroCut X product page rates speed at 24 sheets/minute for two cuts and one crease on an 8 1/2 × 11 sheet. That rating does not measure completed rounded playing-card decks. (low confidence)

Marden Edwards distinguishes LX, LX wide and LXH maximum wrapping rates as 70, 40 and 90 packs per minute, respectively, and explicitly says output depends on pack size. The 90-pack headline cannot be applied to every LX configuration or treated as measured complete-game output. (low confidence)

In a supplier-authored playing-card plant case study, EXAIR reports that cards stuck together and double-fed, and that static regenerated through the process. This is evidence of a real feeding failure mode; it does not establish a universal failure rate or quantified throughput improvement. (low confidence)

TCG Machines documents feed-mechanism adjustment, dirty feed wheels, and insufficient card weight as causes of its PhyzBatch Refill Hopper error. This adjacent card-handling example shows why automated feeding still requires setup and maintenance; its intervals must not be transferred to a manufacturing line. (low confidence)

The CR-50 manual rates Standard/Special cutting units for paper stacks up to 1/2 inch and Large cutting units for stacks up to 1/8 inch. The applicable stack limit depends on the installed cutting-unit class. (low confidence)
Print & Finishing Solutions identifies a nicked blade as a possible cause of ragged slit edges. Treat this as dealer troubleshooting guidance, not a measured failure rate. (low confidence)

In an April 2024 PrintPlanet thread, operator COGordon reported Duplo 646 double-feeding on stocks lighter than card stock despite service-company settings. This is an anecdote about that machine, not a failure-rate measurement or evidence against the DC-746. (low confidence)

Summa documents a recovery path when the camera cannot recognize printed marks: edit the camera profile or select the current position to identify a poorly printed mark. Automatic registration can require operator intervention. (low confidence)

For camera automatic-setup failure, the SmartSlitter manual directs attention to illumination angle and optical focus. Allow troubleshooting effort when evaluating short-run setup burden. (low confidence)

A DC-646 operator reported reliable optical-mark reading on coated substrates but rejection problems on uncoated substrates. This is one attributed stock-dependent failure report, without a verified cause or a population failure-rate estimate. (low confidence)

Rollem describes an Auto-Collator that combines sub-packs into complete sets and an additional in-line cello-wrap unit; this is evidence of a modular collation-to-wrapping workflow, rather than proof that a collator itself loads retail boxes. (low confidence)

Pineberry lists standard CC-50 batch capabilities of 1–100. Its announcement for the 2018 ICMA exhibition additionally says higher counts are available. Treat the higher-count configuration as an unresolved specification. If a proposed stack exceeds the standard batch range, confirm the higher-count configuration rather than assuming the standard counter can process it in one batch. (low confidence)

Uchida specifies EZC-250 items 0.2–0.8mm thick, 25–120mm wide and 40–150mm long, with a stack capacity up to 130mm. Items must be flat, uncurled and without burrs; nonrectangular shapes require testing. These are stock qualification limits rather than proof of compatibility with the game. (low confidence)

Uchida describes Countron OP as an optical counter using an optical sensor and air blow. Its standard TD1 sensor covers 0.18–0.35mm material and its specification says no tab tape insertion. Treat it as quantity-verification equipment, rather than an automatic physical separator for finished decks. (low confidence)

Rollem markets the AutoCollator for lower-volume and short-run card jobs, with collected decks presented to downstream wrapping or packing; these are described as downstream processes rather than functions established by the collator description. (low confidence)

PrintNinja describes a stack smoothing/rounding operation after trimming, while its domestic rotary-die route forms final size and rounded corners together. These are alternative production routes, rather than a requirement that every card use both. (low confidence)

Canon identifies changes in substrate supply or batch as reasons image alignment may need attention and explicitly lists front-versus-back misalignment. Repeated artwork alone does not establish duplex alignment consistency. (low confidence)

Collation, card counting, and banding are distinct operations: Rollem describes arranging cards into decks, Pineberry describes counting individual cards, and Madison describes counting, stacking and banding. Specify which operations a proposed line actually includes. (medium confidence)

The Morgana Countron AT Touch page specifies an optional small-paper attachment with a minimum size of seventy by one hundred sixty millimeters and tab insertion every 2–1,000 sheets. A sheet-counting specification must therefore be checked against the actual finished-card dimensions before selection. (low confidence)

The same EXAIR case study describes a card-production line that boxed and labelled its output. It is an attributed example of downstream boxing automation. If a custom game is proposed, verify its required configuration before using the case-study line as a production model. (low confidence)

Rollem describes SlipStream III collation as collecting rows of cards into sub-decks and sequencing them in a Pack Separation Unit; its software can combine multiple sub-decks so a deck may span multiple sheets or one sheet may produce multiple decks. This is manufacturer-described capability, not verification of the commissioned two-stack game. (low confidence)
Uchida specifies EZC-250 bottom-suction-belt counting at up to two hundred forty pieces per minute, variable; this rating measures counted items, not completed packed games. (low confidence)

Uchida’s dated comparison warns that Countron Touch can curl the counted corner and recommends work where that portion can subsequently be removed. It says Countron AT Touch avoids curling. These are manufacturer statements, not independently demonstrated damage rates. (low confidence)

In its August 02, 2024 comparison, Uchida specifies Countron AT Touch at 80–400gsm, thickness up to 0.4mm depending on stock, and a minimum sheet size of one hundred by one hundred forty-eight millimeters. A heavy-stock counting capability therefore does not establish compatibility with every finished card format. (low confidence)

Uchida’s comparison describes programmable tab insertion at different sheet counts, including successive batches of 48, 24 and 60 sheets. This supports batch separation as a distinct operation; it does not establish card identity or sequence verification. (low confidence)

Duplo markets Esper DM-230V as a direct-mail collator with 23 feed stations and up to 9,000 sets per hour for leaflets, brochures and postcards; the integrated cover wraps a document set. Its described application and input envelope must not be treated as proof of finished small-card deck collation, film wrapping or cartoning. (low confidence)

Jacob White lists semi-automatic and automatic cartoners for playing-card packaging, while stating that machine modifications have constraints based on the customer’s requirements. Listing a compatible machine family does not qualify the commissioned two-stack pack. (low confidence)

Jacob White’s NS-X 3.1 erects cartons automatically on operator demand but leaves product insertion to the operator; after loading, the machine applies glue, closes the flaps and discharges the carton. This is an example of automated carton handling with manual product loading. (low confidence)

Jacob White explicitly makes NS-X 3.1 output dependent on the carton and product, and describes its variable speed range as subject to size and board quality. A finished-game throughput assumption requires the actual pack configuration. (low confidence)

Marden Edwards’ application gallery identifies overwrapped game cards and standard playing-card packs with tear tape. This establishes a manufacturer application example; the gallery provides no demonstrated speed or two-stack loading result for the commissioned game. (low confidence)

In a February 21, 2018 installation announcement, NAPCO/Vulcan says it installed a Rollem MK2 Slipstream and describes inline collation, stacking, boxing and wrapping. Its stated 2,200 decks per hour is an operator-company announcement without a disclosed card-count configuration or independent time study; do not transfer that figure to the commissioned game. (low confidence)

The Game Crafter documents die cutting with rounded corners except on its trading-card format, establishing a card-production route that does not require separately rounding rectangular cuts. (low confidence)

Duplo lists the DC-746 feeder at 150 mm, stock weight at 110–350 gsm, and maxima of 10 slits and 30 cuts per sheet. These are manufacturer specifications for this model, not measured playing-card production results. (low confidence)

In the AeroCut X manual’s MANUSET layout table, gutter H starts at 0.08 inch depending on paper; entering zero requests single cuts. Layout planning must distinguish a removed gutter from a shared cut. (low confidence)

Print & Finishing Solutions warns that heavily static-charged paper can produce misfeeds, double feeds or jams. This dealer’s troubleshooting guidance qualifies expectations of uninterrupted automatic slitting/cutting. (low confidence)

In a December 2021 PrintPlanet discussion about a Duplo 618 cutting crooked, one participant reported similar problems with dirty rollers and said cleaning resolved them. This is an operator anecdote about that model, not a general reliability estimate. (low confidence)

Rollem describes the SlipStream III cutting route as first-direction slitting, with or without bleed, followed by right-angle transfer into the second-direction cutter. This is manufacturer evidence for a two-direction sheet-to-card cutting architecture. (low confidence)
Duplo lists automated job setup and changeovers for the DC-746. (low confidence)
MBM lists a four-inch sheet capacity and a nominal paper-weight range of 120–400 gsm for the AeroCut X. These are manufacturer ratings. (low confidence)
Lassco Wizer lists the CR-55 as a manual foot-operated corner cutter with a two-inch cutting capacity. (low confidence)
Lassco Wizer lists CR-55 blade radii of one-eighth, one-quarter, three-eighths and one-half inch. (low confidence)
The CR-55 manual warns that the bottom card can slide forward and calls for testing on scrap; rated lift capacity alone does not demonstrate a successful card batch. (low confidence)
The CR-55 manual says its blades can dull and can be sharpened. (low confidence)

MBM’s AeroCut X product page displays $43,887 for its slitter, cutter, creaser and perforator. This is a displayed finishing-equipment price; a configured printer-to-boxed-game production-line quote would need separate confirmation of currency, tax, freight and installed-cost inclusions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Duplo documents per-sheet CCD registration-mark reading for horizontal and vertical image-position correction on the DC-618. This is evidence of image-to-finishing alignment capability. (medium confidence)

Duplo says a printed barcode lets the DC-618 CCD scanner recall a stored job and perform the changeover automatically. Its advertised repeat-job automation depends on adding the barcode and registration marks to the artwork. (low confidence)

Hunkeler describes WI8 as print-quality and content inspection: it checks color, position, contour, smearing, jet-outs and data, and compares page images with a golden sample. These are manufacturer specifications, not an independently measured defect-detection rate. (low confidence)

Hunkeler specifies a CIS scan bar per side for WI8 and describes simplex and duplex color integration, including printer-integrated and stand-alone arrangements. The documented application scans a paper web. (low confidence)

In its article dated 26.05.2021, Hunkeler describes golden-template preparation as operator setup work and says IPI instead compares the printed image with production data such as a PDF. The article claims no IPI setup time; this is an attributed vendor-hosted assertion, not measured make-ready time for a game job. (low confidence)

Summa ranks camera alignment to sheet edges as its least accurate markless method. Its more accurate alternative requires manually locating at least 3 recognizable points spread across the cut file. Missing printed marks can therefore leave manual alignment work. (low confidence)

Canon documents printer-side front/back media registration using printed charts and scanner measurements. It stores the resulting adjustment in the media catalog and applies it to jobs using that media; this provides a separate duplex-print calibration step to evaluate alongside finishing registration. (low confidence)

Duplo advertises per-sheet shrinkage and image-position compensation in two axes. A DC-618 forum contributor instead describes shrinkage correction as manual; the thread starter later reports success using the shrinkage setting. These are conflicting attributed accounts, not an established universal automatic-correction result. (medium confidence)

Duplo’s Japanese DC-618 specification lists twenty-three sheets/minute with REG reading off and nineteen with it on for A4 portrait processing with two cuts and one crease. These configuration-specific manufacturer ratings do not establish finished-game throughput or US-model performance. (low confidence)

Hunkeler’s descriptions of golden-sample coverage differ: its WI8 product page describes full-surface comparison, while its explanatory article dated 26.05.2021 characterizes golden templates as selected-point checks. Preserve both descriptions and confirm the purchased inspection configuration before assuming coverage. (low confidence)

Duplo describes barcode-driven program recall and changeover on its DC-618; Horizon also documents barcode-driven job setup for SmartSlitter. This supports repeat-job automation as a manufacturer capability, without establishing elapsed setup time for a game run. (medium confidence)
The SmartSlitter camera operating procedure includes a reference-position setting and a trial sheet feed. Camera automation therefore retains an operator setup step. (low confidence)
